extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, mathematics educators, and administrators designing or implementing quantitative literacy programs
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and running an interdisciplinary undergraduate quantitative literacy (QL) program that ensures all students attain basic quantitative skills by graduation, using a public-policy focal theme and shared campus participation. Includes curricular scope, program structure, learning objectives, faculty support, and assessment-level standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of quantitative literacy (QL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of QL such as: confidence with mathematics, cultural appreciation of the role of data in society, interpreting data, logical thinking, making decisions, mathematics in context, number sense, practical skills, prerequisite knowledge, and symbol sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are the constituent attitudes and abilities that QL instruction should cultivate; all should be addressed in combination with mathematical literacy to achieve QL for every citizen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of life where QL must apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas of life utilizing expressions of QL, such as: citizenship, culture, education, professions, personal finance, personal health, management, and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QL curricula should connect mathematical ideas to these life areas so students can apply quantitative reasoning across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills needed for QL
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills needed for QL, such as: arithmetic, data, computers, modeling, statistics, chance, and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coursework and program offerings should ensure students attain these concrete skills; they form the technical backbone of QL.

rubrics_metrics.name: QL must be integrated across the curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: QL must be everywhere in the curriculum, in all disciplines and all courses, implying that each institution must find its own solution to identifying required QL levels and mechanisms for attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration implies shared responsibility among mathematics faculty, non-mathematics faculty, and administrators to consciously keep QL in classroom conversations and exploit opportunities across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared institutional responsibility for QL
rubrics_metrics.description: In an academic environment, QL is a shared responsibility: mathematics faculty, non-mathematics faculty and administrators are responsible for consciously keeping QL in classroom conversations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful QL initiatives require buy-in from departments, leadership from the mathematics community, professional development, and discussion at national meetings and publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive structure for QL adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a supportive structure that will help to promote buy-in by all disciplines, including strong support and leadership from the mathematics community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because QL lacks its own department or schedule slice, policy changes, influence on textbook/test firms, and incentives for departments are necessary to tip institutional priorities toward QL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for systematic evidence and assessment standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs need systematic evidence to support calls for stronger QL education and clear descriptions of levels of QL and strategies for how they can be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish standards for what constitutes QL at different ages and educational levels to measure progress and justify curricular changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratization of mathematics (accessibility and relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratization of mathematics: making mathematics 'more accessible and responsive to the needs of all students, citizens, and workers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula must coincide with current cultural, political, and economic goals and help every citizen attain a level of QL appropriate to everyday life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity of QL programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Program must be interdisciplinary, involving many different departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary design draws in less-quantitative departments and exposes students to quantitative methods in diverse disciplinary contexts; use a unifying theme to encourage participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-structured and focused program design
rubrics_metrics.description: Program should be well structured and focused, not merely a loose assortment of courses receiving a 'quantitative' designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cohesion (e.g., a common evening meeting) and clear expectations so the program has substantive, assessable goals rather than token status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing courses rather than create many new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Program should be built on existing courses because small colleges have little flexibility to create permanent new courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt current courses and coordinate them through program mechanisms (common meetings, themes) rather than relying on the creation of many new offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie program to institutional strengths (civic engagement/public affairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program should be tied to the institution’s traditional emphases (e.g., Macalester’s civic engagement and interest in public affairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a policy-focused theme that resonates with campus values increases relevance and faculty buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual selection of a unifying public-policy topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year select an important issue as a source of examples of quantitative methods and as a unifying theme for all participating courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rotating policy topic both motivates students (especially 'math averse') and provides a consistent context for interdisciplinary discussion and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common evening class as a shared laboratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an evening time when all students from participating courses come together (a common laboratory section) for lectures, speakers, and discussion tied to the policy issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these meetings to introduce concepts/vocabulary, provide policy background, and bring in speakers; do not attempt to teach technical computation there—techniques are learned within participating courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three broad quantitative topic categories to cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students a survey of fundamental quantitative ideas grouped into Chance (statistical hypothesis testing, sampling, experimental design, measures of correlation), Change (percentages and rates; marginal vs average rates; linear vs exponential growth; importance of units; estimation), and Trade-offs (cost/benefit and cost/effectiveness analysis; other mathematical techniques for comparison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participating courses should expose students to these categories; where full coverage isn't possible in each course, the common meetings can help fill gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary student-centered learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Three program goals: (1) introduce all students to basic quantitative methods in useful context; (2) enable students to think critically about quantitative arguments on public issues; (3) assist faculty to understand and connect quantitative methods to their scholarship and teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second goal (critical critique of quantitative arguments) is central and justifies the requirement that no other course can satisfy the program's graduation requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evening class scope: vocabulary and critique rather than technical training
rubrics_metrics.description: The evening class is designed to acquaint students with the concepts and vocabulary of quantitative analysis and to help students learn how to critique a position paper that relies on quantitative analysis; it does not attempt to teach calculation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical teaching remains the responsibility of participating courses; the common meeting focuses on conceptual understanding and critique skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement and exclusivity for graduation credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in the QM4PP program is intended to be a graduation requirement that cannot be satisfied by any other course in mathematics or any other department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusivity emphasizes the program’s unique combination of interdisciplinary context and critique skills and ensures campus-wide coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development and institutional supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide annual workshops to acquaint faculty with the policy topic and quantitative issues, support personnel to help faculty tie courses to the policy topic, and stipends for faculty adapting courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops (planning and summer) and paid support personnel (a released faculty member and a Policy Associate) are key to scaling participation and helping non-quantitative faculty incorporate quantitative ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic course design given curricular constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that existing courses have full syllabi; rather than forcing every course to cover all topics, use program-level mechanisms (common meetings, speakers, support staff) to achieve breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program must be pragmatic: require some departments to participate, allow voluntary participation for others, and provide support to adapt courses without overloading existing syllabi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment focus on critique and vocabulary rather than procedural mastery in common meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: The program’s evening class and common elements should aim to develop the ability to critique quantitative arguments, know the basic terminology, and identify questions to judge validity; deeper measurement or computation is taught in home courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment and learning objectives should therefore measure conceptual understanding, critical questioning, and ability to interpret quantitative claims in public discourse.
